𝗜 𝗟𝗜𝗞𝗘 𝗨𝗦𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗖𝗥𝗬𝗣𝗧𝗢 𝗕𝗘𝗖𝗔𝗨𝗦𝗘 𝗜 𝗛𝗔𝗩𝗘 𝗠𝗢𝗥𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗢𝗟 𝗢𝗩𝗘𝗥 𝗠𝗬 𝗠𝗢𝗡𝗘𝗬.

But there's one thing that has always bothered me about public blockchains.
Once someone knows my wallet address, they can look through my transaction history, see how much I'm holding and track where my money goes.

That information isn't something I'd casually share with strangers in real life. So why should using crypto mean giving up that privacy?

This is one of the problems @zolanacom is trying to solve.
To understand what makes Zolana interesting, let's look at the privacy trade-offs in existing blockchains.

𝗙𝗜𝗥𝗦𝗧, 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘'𝗦 @Zcash .

Zcash allows users to make shielded transactions that hide the sender, recipient and transaction amount.
However, its average block time is around 75 seconds.

𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘'𝗦 @solana .

Solana offers much faster transaction processing, but privacy tools operating within its environment face different technical constraints.

Take Helius's default Privacy Ring, for example. It hides the asset and transaction amount, but the sender and recipient remain publicly visible.

So, while some transaction details are protected, the identities of the parties involved aren't necessarily hidden.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗕𝗥𝗜𝗡𝗚𝗦 𝗨𝗦 𝗧𝗢 @zolanacom .

Zolana is attempting to combine Zcash-style payment privacy with a high-performance blockchain architecture.

But it isn't simply building another privacy application on Solana.
Zolana takes a different approach by building privacy directly into its own Layer 1 blockchain.
It introduces something called shielded payments.

𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘'𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗠𝗘𝗔𝗡𝗦 𝗜𝗡 𝗦𝗜𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘 𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗠𝗦:

When I send someone money through a shielded payment, the amount I'm sending and the recipient's private receiving address aren't exposed on the public ledger.

Instead of revealing those details, my wallet creates a cryptographic proof.

Think of this proof as a way of showing that a transaction is valid without revealing all the private information behind it.

𝗕𝗨𝗧 𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗧𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗞 𝗞𝗡𝗢𝗪 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗦𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗜𝗦 𝗟𝗘𝗚𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗘?

This is where Zolana's architecture becomes interesting.
Zolana uses Orchard, a shielded-payment system that relies on zero-knowledge proofs.
These proofs are relatively large, making them difficult to fit within the constraints of an ordinary Solana program.

Rather than forcing the entire privacy mechanism into a Solana program, Zolana integrates proof verification directly into its own validators.

This allows validators to check whether a shielded transaction follows the network's rules without needing to see the private payment details.
Orchard also uses Halo 2 proofs, which don't require a trusted setup.

𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘'𝗦 𝗔𝗡𝗢𝗧𝗛𝗘𝗥 𝗗𝗘𝗧𝗔𝗜𝗟 𝗪𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗛 𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗜𝗡𝗚:

 Users can pay transaction fees directly from their shielded funds.
This means they don't necessarily need to expose a separate public balance just to pay for a private transaction.

Of course, privacy doesn't mean every piece of information disappears. Transaction timing, fees, nullifiers and certain other metadata can still be public.

But the underlying idea is important.
Using crypto shouldn't automatically mean making your entire financial history available for strangers to inspect.

Zolana is working towards making private payments a native part of blockchain infrastructure.
Because financial freedom should include the freedom to keep your financial activities private.
